# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–28 (Complete – Updated 201)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Winter of seventh year after Waterloo**. John Sedley deceased (died peacefully in sleep; buried at Brompton churchyard beside wife). Mr. Osborne deceased (died four days after stroke; found at foot of dressing-table). Major Dobbin appointed executor of Osborne's will. Rawdon governs Coventry Island. Georgy established as heir. **Continental tour progressing**: Amelia, Georgy, Jos, and Major Dobbin on steamship and carriage tour; landed Rotterdam, traveled to Cologne, now established in Pumpernickel (a small German principality) for autumn/winter season. **Year noted as 1830 (French Revolution occurred this year)**.
- **Major locations**: London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Gaunt House, Regent Club, Knightsbridge Barracks, Russell Square, Brompton, Conduit Street, Hart Street Bloomsbury, Southampton Row, Kensington Gardens, Camberwell, Slaughters' Inn, Haymarket Theatre, Gillespie Street); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate (deed to pastures discovered to be forged by Madrek Orlwood; Feena Stenworth found work there and did not return); Piccadilly; Madras; St. Helena; Cape; Southampton; Staveton; Belgium (Brussels, Mount St. John, Waterloo, Laeken); Bengal; Salford; Regent's Park; Richmond (Star and Garter); Gulton; Harrowgate; Hill farms; Roehampton; Hampton Court; Calcutta; Jamaica; Rotterdam; Cologne; Free City of Judenstadt; Rhine region; Rhineland; **Pumpernickel** (small German principality with Court, theatre, Duke's schloss, Prime Minister's lodgings, Aurelius Platz, Zwieback's Conditorey, Saint Michael's Fountain, Artillery Place, Stadthaus, Town Hall, Redoute, gardens with Trophonius' cave, nymphbath, Niagara cataract); Mirecombe; Dunholt; Dunwick; Quenwick; Humbourg-Schlippenschloppen; Ems; Aix-la-Chapelle; Baden-Baden; **Salwick** (bridge toll skimmed monthly – reported by Madrek Orlwood to Movie); Elephant (lodging-house, Room No. 90/92); Boulogne; Dieppe; Portman Square; Brussels; Paris; Wildbad; Strasburg; St. Petersburg; Toplitz; Vienna; Pincian Hill (Rome); Naples; Castle Gaunt; Trinity House; White Friars; Chiswick; University of Schoppenhausen; Leipzig; Dresden; Schoppenhausen; Clapham; **Miremere** (Fedette Orlwood planned journey before frost, postponed due to flooded roads).

## Rebecca at Pumpernickel – Gaming and Seduction (Chapters 27–28)

**Arrival and Gaming Encounters**: At Stadthaus gaming, Jos remained at play-table. Woman in foreign accent revealed herself as **Rebecca (Madame de Raudon)**, formerly involved with Rawdon Crawley. Spoke of seeing "dear Amelia," noted she "looked pretty and happy."

**Seduction of Jos (Chapter 28)**: Rebecca in pink domino (faded, soiled) led Jos into garret at Elephant lodging-house (Room No. 92). Hid evidence of degradation (rouge-pot, brandy bottle, plate of broken meat), smoothed hair. Gave tender looks, claimed heart first learned to beat at Jos's presence; denied giving George encouragement; asserted marital duties paramount; promised preserve virtue "to her dying day, or until...Colonel Crawley's...cruelty had rendered odious." Jos departed convinced "that she was the most virtuous, as she was one of the most fascinating of women" and resolved she must quit that place, take quiet lodging, and that Amelia must befriend her.

**Becky's True Nature**: After Jos departed, "Becky bowed Jos out of her little garret with as much grace as if it was a palace of which she did the honours." Max and Fritz (students from Schoppenhausen) came out of hole, pipe in mouth. She mimicked Jos while munching cold bread and sausage and drinking brandy-and-water. **Becky liked the life**: "She was at home with everybody in the place, pedlars, punters, tumblers, students and all. She was of a wild, roving nature, inherited from father and mother, who were both Bohemians, by taste and circumstance." Students reported: Becky advertised concert at Leipzig that did not occur (claimed pianist fell ill at Dresden). She won money at trente-et-quarante using young Georgy to play for her; planned to spend money on wine, theatre, or Cognac in Aurelius Garden rather than buy her own concert tickets.

## Jos and Dobbin's Conflict (Chapter 28)

Jos walked to Dobbin's lodgings with great solemnity and imparted affecting history without mentioning gaming. Two gentlemen consulted as to best means of being useful to Mrs. Becky.

**Major's Distrust and Jos's Resentment**: When Major heard from Jos, excitement was "quite the reverse from a pleasurable one"; he called her "The little minx." Never had slightest liking for her; heartily mistrusted her from first moment when "her green eyes had looked at, and turned away from, his own." Said: "That little devil brings mischief wherever she goes." Questioned who knows what sort of life she has been leading, why abroad and alone, why left husband. Recalled Rawdon was "confounded blackleg" who cheated poor George. Remembered scandal about separation. Jos tried in vain to convince Dobbin that Mrs. Becky was "in all respects a most injured and virtuous female."

Jos became "not a little jealous of the airs of superiority which the Major constantly exhibited towards him" (Jos imparted opinions to Mr. Kirsch, the courier, whose bills Major Dobbin checked on journey, and who sided with Jos). Jos began blustering speech about his competency to defend his own honour, his desire not to have his affairs meddled with, his intention to rebel against the Major. Colloquy—"rather a long and stormy one"—ended simply by arrival of Mrs. Becky with porter from Elephant Hotel in charge of her meagre baggage.

## Amelia's Embrace of Rebecca; Major's Rejection (Chapter 28)

**Becky's Arrival and Greeting**: She greeted Jos with affectionate respect and made shrinking, but amicable salutation to Major Dobbin, who—as her instinct assured her at once—was her enemy and had been speaking against her.

**Amelia's Warmth; Dobbin's Departure**: Emmy embraced her guest with greatest warmth, took no notice of the Major except to fling him "an angry look—the most unjust and scornful glance that had perhaps ever appeared in that poor little woman's face since she was born." She had private reasons of her own and was bent upon being angry with him. Dobbin, indignant at injustice, made her a bow quite as haughty as the killing curtsey with which Emmy bid him farewell. He departed.

**Emmy's Bustling Hospitality**: Emmy was particularly lively and affectionate to Rebecca, bustled about apartments and installed her guest with eagerness and activity seldom exhibited by placid little friend. Emmy thought she was displaying great deal of firmness and proper feeling and veneration for late Captain Osborne in her present behaviour.

**Becky's False Narrative**: Amelia's frankness and kindness touched Becky. She returned Emmy's caresses with "something very like gratitude, and an emotion which, if it was not lasting, for a moment was almost genuine." Becky claimed child "torn from her arms shrieking." Amelia cried out: "Oh, Rebecca, my poor dear suffering friend, I know what it is to lose a boy...But please Heaven yours will be restored to you, as a merciful merciful Providence has brought me back mine."

Becky owned to agonies regarding child "not perhaps without a twinge of conscience." Becky gave full version: marriage with Rawdon viewed by family with utmost hostility; sister-in-law (artful woman) poisoned husband's mind against her; he formed odious connections, estranged affections; she bore everything—poverty, neglect, coldness "for the sake of her child"; finally driven to demand separation when wretch asked she sacrifice fair fame for advancement through Marquis of Steyne—"The atrocious monster!" Forced to flee by insult; coward pursued revenge by taking child from her. Emmy received story with indignation and offered: "She may have Payne's room...The poor creature, after all her sufferings...quite alone and absolutely forced to give lessons in singing to get her bread—and not have her here!"

## Georgy Meets Becky; Dinner Scene (Chapter 28)

Georgy came in from fetes for dinner-time and found four covers laid; one place occupied by Rebecca instead of by Major Dobbin. "Hullo! where's Dob?" Amelia said Major was dining out, kissed Georgy a great deal, put his hair off his forehead, introduced him to Mrs. Crawley. Becky looked at him with rapture and pressed his hand fondly. "Dear boy!" she said—"he is just like my--" Emotion choked her utterance, but Amelia understood Becky was thinking of her own blessed child. She ate a very good dinner.

During repast, Georgy eyed Becky and listened to her. At dessert Emmy was gone out to superintend domestic arrangements; Jos was in his great chair dozing over Galignani. Georgy and Becky sat close to each other—he looked at her knowingly more than once, and at last he laid down the nutcrackers.

## Major Dobbin's Departure (Chapter 28)

**Dobbin's Eavesdropping and Rebecca's Note**: Whilst Dobbin and Amelia had been talking, Becky kept hold of the door handle into Mrs. Osborne's room and heard every word of their conversation. "What a noble heart that man has," she thought, "and how shamefully that woman plays with it!" She admired Dobbin; bore him no rancour. "Ah! if I could have had such a husband as that--a man with a heart and brains too! I would not have minded his large feet." She wrote him a note beseeching him to stop for a few days—not to think of going—and that she could serve him with A. [note text incomplete in source].

**Departure Scene**: William got into carriage, released from embraces of landlord. George bounded in afterwards, flung his arms round the Major's neck, began asking him multiplied questions. Then he felt in his waistcoat pocket and gave him a note. William seized it rather eagerly, opened it trembling, but instantly his countenance changed, and he tore the paper in two and dropped it out of the carriage. He kissed Georgy on the head, and the boy got out, doubling his fists into his eyes, aided by Francis. William lingered with his hand on the panel. "Fort, Schwager!" The yellow postilion cracked his whip prodigiously, up sprang Francis to the box, away went the schimmels, and Dobbin with his head on his breast. He never looked up as they passed under Amelia's window, and Georgy, left alone in the street, burst out crying.

**Dobbin's Final Speech and Rejection of Amelia (Chapter 28)**: William had said sadly: "You don't mean that these words, uttered in a hurried moment, are to weigh against a whole life's devotion? I think that George's memory has not been injured by the way in which I have dealt with it, and if we are come to bandying reproaches, I at least merit none from his widow and the mother of his son."

He continued: "It is not that speech of yesterday which moves you. That is but the pretext, Amelia, or I have loved you and watched you for fifteen years in vain. Have I not learned in that time to read all your feelings and look into your thoughts? I know what your heart is capable of: it can cling faithfully to a recollection and cherish a fancy, but it can't feel such an attachment as mine deserves to mate with...No, you are not worthy of the love which I have devoted to you. I knew all along that the prize I had set my life on was not worth the winning...I will bargain no more: I withdraw...Good-bye, Amelia! I have watched your struggle. Let it end. We are both weary of it."

**Amelia's Loss**: Amelia stood scared and silent as William broke the chain by which she held him and declared his independence and superiority. He had placed himself at her feet so long that the poor little woman had been accustomed to trample upon him. "She didn't wish to marry him, but she wished to keep him. She wished to give him nothing, but that he should give her all."

## Becky Established in Household (Chapter 28)

**Rebecca's Reflection on Dobbin**: Whatever Becky's private plan might be by which Dobbin's true love was to be crowned with success, the little woman thought that the secret might keep, being by no means so much interested about anybody's welfare as about her own, she had a great number of things pertaining to herself to consider, which concerned her a great deal more than Major Dobbin's happiness in this life.

**Becky's Contentment**: She found herself suddenly and unexpectedly in snug comfortable quarters, surrounded by friends, kindness, and good-natured simple people such as she had not met with for many a long day; and, wanderer as she was by force and inclination, there were moments when rest was pleasant to her. "As the most hardened Arab that ever careered across the desert over the hump of a dromedary likes to repose sometimes under the date-trees by the water, or to come into the cities, walk into the bazaars, refresh himself in the baths, and say his prayers in the mosques, before he goes out again marauding, so Jos's tents and pilau were pleasant to this little Ishmaelite. She picketed her steed, hung up her weapons, and warmed herself comfortably by his fire."

**Jos Enslaved; Emmy Manipulated**: In course of a week, Jos was her sworn slave and frantic admirer. He didn't go to sleep after dinner as his custom was. He drove out with Becky in his open carriage. He asked little parties and invented festivities to do her honour. As for Emmy, who found herself not in the least mistress of her own house except when bills were to be paid, Becky soon discovered the way to soothe and please her. She talked perpetually about Major Dobbin sent about his business, made no scruple of declaring her admiration for that excellent, high-minded gentleman, and of telling Emmy that she had behaved most cruelly regarding him. Emmy defended her conduct but had no objection to hear the Major praised as much as ever Becky chose to praise him, and indeed, brought the conversation round to the Dobbin subject a score of times every day.

**Servants and Georgy Won Over**: Amelia's maid was heart and soul in favour of the generous Major. Having at first disliked Becky for dismissing him from presence of her mistress, she was reconciled to Mrs. Crawley subsequently, because the latter became William's most ardent admirer and champion. In nightly conclaves whilst "brushing their 'airs," the girl always put in her word for that dear good gentleman Major Dobbin. Her advocacy did not make Amelia angry any more than Rebecca's admiration of him. Emmy made George write to him constantly and persisted in sending Mamma's kind love in a postscript.

**Amelia's Unhappiness**: Emmy was not very happy after her heroic sacrifice. She was very distraite, nervous, silent, and ill to please. The family had never known her so peevish. She grew pale and ill. She used to try to sing certain songs (including "Einsam bin ich nicht alleine," that tender love-song of Weber's) to which the Major was partial; and as she warbled them in the twilight in the drawing-room, she would break off in the midst of the song, and walk into her neighbouring apartment, and there, no doubt, take refuge in the miniature of her husband.

## Key Character States (End of Chapter 28)
- **Amelia**: Rejected Dobbin's love; now suffers regret and unhappiness; distrait, nervous, silent, peevish; grows pale and ill; has lost her devoted follower; manipulated by Becky into praising Dobbin while keeping him absent.
- **Major Dobbin**: Departed Pumpernickel definitively; ended fifteen years of hidden love and devoted service; declared Amelia unworthy; tore up Becky's note without reading it fully; left with head on breast, did not look back.
- **Rebecca**: Secured comfortable quarters in Amelia's household; enslaved Jos within a week through charm and manipulation; manipulated Emmy by praising Dobbin while keeping him at distance; won over servants and Georgy; considers her own welfare paramount; enjoys the rest and stability but remains fundamentally Bohemian in nature.
- **Jos Sedley**: Enslaved to Becky; drives out with her in open carriage; invents festivities to do her honour; is her "sworn slave and frantic admirer."
- **Georgy**: Attentive to Becky; sits close to her at dinner; receives correspondence from Dobbin via mother; impressed by her presence.
- **Rawdon Crawley**: Separated permanently from Rebecca; financially settled on three hundred pounds per year with understanding she never trouble him again; transformed morally; governs Coventry Island.
